procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals (Civil Appeal Nos. 3642-3646 of 2018) filed by the Appellants (Akshay & Anr.) finding them to be devoid of merit.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants were liable for the acts of Respondent No. 2, even after the revocation of the power of attorney, given that the underlying Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) was not revoked?

facts: The appellants (landowners) and Respondent No. 2 (a builder) entered into a Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) and an irrevocable Power of Attorney (POA) on July 6, 2013, for the development of land.
Under the authority of these agreements, Respondent No. 2 entered into sale agreements with the complainants for units in the project.
On August 12, 2014, the appellants sent a letter claiming to revoke the POA.
The complainants filed a case against both the appellants and Respondent No. 2 for deficiency of service, seeking joint and several liability.
law: The liability of a principal (the landowners) for the acts of their agent (the builder) is determined by the scope and duration of the authority granted.
The revocation of a Power of Attorney does not necessarily terminate the underlying agreement (like a JVA) that granted the authority in the first place.
The effect of a revocation is determined by its specific terms and timing; it may only apply prospectively (to future acts) and not retroactively.
application: The Court first established that while the appellants claimed to have revoked the Power of Attorney, the underlying Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) was never revoked and remained in force. This JVA was the source of the builder's authority to develop and sell the property.

The Court then analyzed the appellants' own revocation letter from August 12, 2014. It highlighted that the letter stated the appellants would not be liable "Henceforth," meaning only for acts committed *after* that date.

It was noted that the builder (Respondent No. 2) had entered into the agreements with the complainants *before* the date of the revocation letter. At the time these agreements were made, both the JVA and the irrevocable POA were fully operative.

Therefore, the Court reasoned that the appellants were bound by all acts and deeds carried out by the builder pursuant to the POA up until the point it was terminated. The revocation did not erase liability for actions already taken under its authority.

The Court also observed that the appellants had not taken any legal action against the builder for any alleged breaches of the JVA, which weakened their attempt to distance themselves from the builder's actions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellants were liable for the acts of Respondent No. 2. The Court's reasoning was that the underlying Joint Venture Agreement was never revoked, and the revocation of the power of attorney only applied to future acts ("Henceforth"). Since the builder entered into agreements with the complainants while the JVA and POA were still in full force, the appellants could not escape their joint liability for those actions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants were liable for the acts of Respondent No. 2, even after the revocation of the power of attorney, given that the underlying Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) was not revoked?
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that they were not liable for the acts of Respondent No. 2 after they issued a letter revoking the power of attorney on 12-8-2014.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that the revocation letter itself stated the appellants would not be liable 'henceforth,' implying liability for prior acts remained.
The agreements with the complainants were entered into before the power of attorney was revoked.
The underlying Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) between the appellants and Respondent No. 2, which formed the basis of their relationship, was never cancelled.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A principal who has entered into a Joint Venture Agreement and granted an irrevocable Power of Attorney to an agent remains bound by the agent's acts carried out pursuant to that power of attorney until it is lawfully terminated. The revocation of the power of attorney only has prospective effect and does not absolve the principal of liability for the agent's actions, particularly when the underlying Joint Venture Agreement remains in force.
obiter: When a lower adjudicatory body, such as the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC), has considered all issues regarding the joint liability of the parties, the Supreme Court may find no good ground to interfere with its decision.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellants, as landowners, cannot escape their liability for the acts of their joint venture partner because the underlying Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) was never revoked and continued to be in force. The subsequent revocation of the power of attorney only operated prospectively, as indicated by the use of the word "Henceforth" in the revocation letter, meaning the appellants remained bound by the acts and deeds carried out by their partner before the termination.
legal_tests_applied: The court did not apply a formal, named legal test but instead engaged in a contractual analysis, examining the continuing legal effect of the Joint Venture Agreement and the prospective-only effect of the power of attorney's revocation.
why_appellant_lost: The Joint Venture Agreement (JVA), which was the basis of the relationship, was not revoked and continued to be in force.
The letter revoking the power of attorney stated the appellants would not be liable "Henceforth," which implicitly confirmed their liability for acts that occurred prior to the letter.
The agreements with the complainants were made before the power of attorney was revoked, at a time when the JVA and the power of attorney were both fully operative.
The appellants were bound by the acts and deeds of Respondent No. 2 that were carried out pursuant to the power of attorney up until the point it was terminated.
why_respondent_won: The JVA between the appellants and Respondent No. 2 was never cancelled, meaning their joint liability remained intact.
The agreements with the complainants were entered into while the power of attorney granted by the appellants to Respondent No. 2 was still valid and operative.
The appellants' own revocation letter limited their non-liability to future acts ("Henceforth"), thereby not absolving them of responsibility for prior agreements made with the complainants.
policy_considerations: Allowing the landowners to escape liability would result in grave injustice to the complainants/consumers.
The appellants/landowners cannot be allowed to wash their hands of the matter and escape their responsibility in providing relief to the consumers.
